title: Fold an outlet's three stiff copper wires back into its wall box and seat the outlet
instruction: Put the outlet back in its wall box, ready for its screws, with every wire inside the box. Then let go.
context: Putting a receptacle back in its box is routine for electricians (O*NET 47-2111.00, 821,000 US jobs in 2025: "Assemble, install, test, or maintain electrical or electronic wiring, equipment, appliances, apparatus, or fixtures, using hand tools or power tools") and general maintenance and repair workers (49-9071.00, 1,621,800 jobs: "Assemble, install, or repair wiring, electrical or electronic components, pipe systems, plumbing, machinery, or equipment"). The wires are solid 12 AWG copper: they keep whatever bend they are given and push back. Pushed straight in, their loops stand up over the box's top edge and are trapped between the outlet and the wall, where a pinched conductor is a shock and fire risk. Each loop has to be folded into the box while the other hand holds the outlet, and only then will the outlet go home. No screws are driven: the task ends with the outlet let go, sitting where its screws would reach.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table: x forward (away from the robot), y to the robot's left; heights above the table. Wall (fixed, off-white board): 32 cm wide, 30 cm tall, 1.27 cm thick, standing on the table with its front face at x 37.5, from y -24 to y +8. Wall box (fixed, blue plastic, open to the front, its rim flush with the wall's face): inside 5.2 cm wide, 9.0 cm tall and 6.6 cm deep, walls 2.5 mm thick, opening centred at y -8, 19 cm up. Inside it, on the centre line, a screw boss 1.0 cm wide stands 0.67 cm in from the top wall and another from the bottom wall; their screw holes are 8.33 cm apart. Outlet (loose, 70 g): a steel mounting strap 3.35 cm wide, 10.67 cm tall and 1.5 mm thick; an ivory plastic body 3.35 cm wide, 6.8 cm tall and 2.0 cm deep behind the strap; an ivory face 3.35 cm wide, 6.8 cm tall and 0.45 cm thick in front of it. It is not connected to power, and the strap's edges are deburred so they cannot cut the gripper pads. It hangs on its wires, upright, facing the robot, centred on the opening, with the back of its strap 11.5 cm in front of the wall. Wires (three, solid 12 AWG copper, conductor 2.05 mm across, cut fresh for every trial): one black and one white, insulated to 3.0 mm across, each 20.3 cm (8 in) long from the cable entry to its terminal, and one bare, 19.2 cm long. All three are fixed side by side at the cable entry at the top back of the box, 5.8 cm behind the wall's face, 3 cm above the opening's centre (the bare wire 2.6 cm) and 0.75 to 1.65 cm to the left of it. The black wire ends on the right side of the outlet's body and the white wire on its left side, both 1.2 cm above the outlet's centre; the bare wire ends on the left side, 3.0 cm below the centre. Each wire has two folds bent into it before it is fitted, each a V standing 9 mm off the wire's line over 32 mm of wire. On the black and the white wire: one 7.0 cm from the terminal, pointing up, and one 13.8 cm from the terminal, pointing down and to the robot's right. On the bare wire: one 7.3 cm from the terminal, pointing down, and one 13.5 cm from the terminal, pointing down and to the robot's right. Between its ends each wire runs in a shallow S, dipping below the straight line near the box's mouth and rising above it nearer the outlet. wire_start_points.csv lists each wire's path every 5 mm and wire_start_shapes.pdf is a 1:1 template of it (side and top views). Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Measured on the last step from the outlet's pose, 20 or 21 points along each wire, and the grippers' positions. Score 0 unless all of these hold: the outlet is upright (its long axis within 15 degrees of vertical); every corner of its strap is within 15 mm of the wall's face (near enough for a 1 in mounting screw to reach its hole); every wire is inside the box (no point of a wire more than 2 mm in front of the wall's face, apart from the last 5 mm at the outlet's terminal, which is part of the outlet; and no point outside the opening's outline within 3 mm of the face); and the outlet has been let go (the grip centre and pad tips of both grippers at least 3 cm from the outlet and from every wire, with the outlet moving under 1 cm/s, for the last 2 s). Then: 1.0 if both of the strap's screw holes are within 3 mm of the box's screw holes, measured across the wall; 0.5 if either is further off. Doing nothing, a push that leaves a wire trapped or showing, and an outlet still held or pressed in place all score 0. On a real rig the strap's corners and the screw holes are measured with a ruler, and the wire rule is read from three photos taken once the grippers are away: one square-on from the front, and one along the wall's face from each side, level with the opening's centre, with a strip 2 mm thick stuck to the wall 3 cm below the opening as the reference. A wire fails if, anywhere other than the last 5 mm at its terminal, more than half its thickness stands further from the wall than the strip's face in a side photo, or if any part of it lies on the wall or the box's rim outside the opening in any photo. A scoring outlet is within 15 mm of the wall and its body is as wide as its strap, so the two side photos between them show all of the space in front of the wall, behind the strap included. Any part of a wire that no photo shows is therefore behind the wall's face, inside the box, which is where the rule wants it: wire hidden behind the outlet cannot break the rule unseen.
reset_notes: Every trial starts with fresh wire, so the starting shape and stiffness are the same each time. Cut three new lengths from the same reels (free lengths 20.3, 20.3 and 19.2 cm, plus what the entry clamp and the terminal screw take). Mark each fold's place from the terminal end and bend it once on a three-pin block (two 6 mm pins 32 mm apart and a third midway) until the V stands 9 mm off the wire's line, within 1 mm. Fit each wire to its terminal and the cable entry with its folds pointing as the setup lists, pull the outlet out until the back of its strap is 11.5 cm in front of the wall, and shape each wire by hand against the 1:1 template (wire_start_shapes.pdf) until it follows it to within 3 mm. About 5 minutes. Used wires are thrown away, never straightened and used again: copper work-hardens where it is bent, so only new wire bent once the same way starts with the same stiffness. In the simulator every reset restores this shape and each fold's starting hardening, with nothing carried over from the last trial.
fidelity: Each wire is a chain of rigid links 10.7 mm long on two-axis joints that bend like solid 12 AWG copper: stiffness from E 117 GPa, first yield at 59 N mm, and work hardening from annealed copper's stress-strain curve, so a bend stays and gets harder to bend further. Each starting fold begins hardened by the bend it holds, as new wire bent once is. Twist along a wire and stretch are left out. The outlet, box and wall are rigid and true size.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 after 2,400 steps (termination: step limit); scripted demo: 1.0 after 1,352 steps (termination: success)
